Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

Workplace safety in hazardous environments like construction sites and industrial plants is crucial to prevent accidents and injuries. One of the most important safety measures is ensuring workers wear safety helmets, which protect against head injuries from falling objects and machinery. Non-compliance with helmet regulations increases the risk of serious injuries or fatalities, making effective monitoring essential, especially in large-scale operations where manual oversight is prone to errors and inefficiency.

To overcome these challenges, SafeGuard Corp plans to develop an automated image analysis system capable of detecting whether workers are wearing safety helmets. This system will improve safety enforcement, ensuring compliance and reducing the risk of head injuries. By automating helmet monitoring, SafeGuard aims to enhance efficiency, scalability, and accuracy, ultimately fostering a safer work environment while minimizing human error in safety oversight.

Objective¶

As a data scientist at SafeGuard Corp, you are tasked with developing an image classification model that classifies images into one of two categories:

  • With Helmet: Workers wearing safety helmets.
  • Without Helmet: Workers not wearing safety helmets.

Data Description¶

The dataset consists of 4125 images, divided into two categories:

  • With Helmet: 3161 images showing workers wearing helmets.
  • Without Helmet: 964 images showing workers not wearing helmets.

Dataset Characteristics:

  • Variations in Conditions: Images include diverse environments such as construction sites, factories, and industrial settings, with variations in lighting, angles, and worker postures to simulate real-world conditions.
  • Worker Activities: Workers are depicted in different actions such as standing, using tools, or moving, ensuring robust model learning for various scenarios.

Exploratory Data Analysis: Random Image Samples¶

This visualization provides an exploratory check of the image data. It helps confirm that the images and labels were loaded correctly and that the two classes generally represent their intended categories.

How to Read the Display¶

  • The left column contains randomly selected images labeled 1, meaning With Helmet.
  • The right column contains randomly selected images labeled 0, meaning Without Helmet.
  • The index displayed in each title identifies the image's position in the dataset. It is not a model prediction or performance score.
  • Five images were randomly selected from each class.

For example:

  • With Helmet (Index: 1092) means that image 1092 has a true label of 1.
  • Without Helmet (Index: 360) means that image 360 has a true label of 0.

What the Code Does¶

The following line identifies the positions of all images labeled 1:

helmet_indices = labels[labels.iloc[:, 0] == 1].index.tolist()

The following line identifies the positions of all images labeled 0:

no_helmet_indices = labels[labels.iloc[:, 0] == 0].index.tolist()

The following command randomly selects five images from the helmet class:

random.sample(helmet_indices, 5)

The same process is used to select five images from the no-helmet class. The loop then displays the selected images in two columns for visual comparison.

Observations¶

The sampled images suggest that the class labels are generally reasonable:

  • Workers in the left column are wearing visible red, yellow, or white safety helmets.
  • People in the right column generally have uncovered heads rather than safety helmets.
  • The dataset includes front, side, and rear views of workers.
  • Helmet colors, shapes, and visibility vary.
  • The size and location of each person's head vary considerably.
  • Some images contain more than one person.
  • Lighting conditions and backgrounds vary across the dataset.
  • Several images are blurred, low-resolution, partially obstructed, or poorly framed.
  • Some workers occupy only a small portion of the image.

The helmet image at index 3892 is particularly blurred, making the helmet difficult to distinguish. Some no-helmet images are also blurred or partially obstructed. These difficult examples could increase classification errors.

Important Interpretation¶

This visualization does not demonstrate that a model is accurate because no model has been trained or evaluated yet. It only helps confirm that:

  1. The image array and label file appear to be correctly aligned.
  2. Label 1 represents With Helmet.
  3. Label 0 represents Without Helmet.
  4. The dataset contains considerable visual variability.
  5. Some images may be difficult even for a human to classify.

Overall EDA Conclusion¶

The sampled images confirm that label 1 represents workers wearing safety helmets and label 0 represents workers without safety helmets. The dataset contains substantial variation in helmet color, worker position, head orientation, lighting, background, image sharpness, and camera distance.

Several images are blurred, partially obstructed, or contain small subjects, which may make classification difficult. This variability reflects realistic image conditions, but it may also increase model error—particularly when a worker's head or helmet is not clearly visible.

Concise Observation for the Presentation¶

Random samples confirmed the intended class definitions. The images vary considerably in lighting, viewing angle, subject size, background, and sharpness. Blurred and partially obstructed images represent challenging classification cases and may reduce model performance.

Exploratory Data Analysis: Class Distribution¶

This count plot shows the number of images belonging to each target class in the dataset.

How to Read the Chart¶

  • The red bar represents images labeled 0, meaning Without Helmet.
  • The green bar represents images labeled 1, meaning With Helmet.
  • The number above each bar is the exact number of images in that class.

The dataset contains:

  • 964 images without helmets
  • 3,161 images with helmets
  • 4,125 total images

Class Percentages¶

The percentage of images in each class is calculated as:

$$ \text{Class Percentage} = \frac{\text{Number of Images in the Class}} {\text{Total Number of Images}} \times 100 $$

For the Without Helmet class:

$$ \frac{964}{4125}\times 100 \approx 23.4\% $$

For the With Helmet class:

$$ \frac{3161}{4125}\times 100 \approx 76.6\% $$

Therefore:

  • Without Helmet (0): approximately 23.4%
  • With Helmet (1): approximately 76.6%

There are approximately:

$$ \frac{3161}{964}\approx3.28 $$

times as many helmet images as no-helmet images. Therefore:

  • Without Helmet (0): approximately 23.4%
  • With Helmet (1): approximately 76.6%

There are approximately 3.28 times as many helmet images as no-helmet images.

What the Code Does¶

The following statement creates a figure measuring 6 inches wide by 4 inches high:

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))

The following command counts the number of examples associated with each label and displays the results as bars:

ax = sns.countplot(
    x=labels.iloc[:, 0],
    palette=["red", "green"]
)

In this expression, labels.iloc[:, 0] selects every row from the first column of the labels DataFrame.

The following loop places the exact class count above each bar:

for p in ax.patches:
    ax.annotate(
        f"{int(p.get_height())}",
        (
            p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2,
            p.get_height()
        ),
        ha="center",
        va="bottom",
        fontsize=10
    )

The remaining commands add the chart title, axis labels, and descriptive class names.

Observations¶

The chart reveals a noticeable class imbalance:

  • The With Helmet class is the majority class.
  • The Without Helmet class is the minority class.
  • More than three-quarters of the images belong to the helmet class.
  • Less than one-quarter belong to the no-helmet class.

This imbalance could cause a model to favor the majority class. For example, a model that predicted With Helmet for every image would obtain approximately 76.6% accuracy, even though it would fail to identify every unsafe no-helmet case.

Therefore, accuracy alone will not provide an adequate evaluation of model performance.

Modeling Implications¶

The data should be divided using a stratified split so that the training, validation, and test sets preserve approximately the same class proportions.

Model performance should be evaluated using multiple measures, including:

  • Macro precision
  • Macro recall
  • Macro F1-score
  • Confusion matrix
  • Recall for the Without Helmet class
  • Recall for the With Helmet class

Recall for the Without Helmet class is particularly important because failing to detect a worker without a helmet could allow an unsafe condition to go unaddressed.

A standard binary recall metric usually treats label 1 as the positive class. In this dataset, label 1 means With Helmet. Therefore, standard recall for label 1 does not directly measure the model's ability to detect unsafe no-helmet cases. Class-specific recall and the confusion matrix should also be examined.

Overall EDA Conclusion¶

The dataset is imbalanced, with 3,161 helmet images and 964 no-helmet images. The helmet class accounts for approximately 76.6% of the dataset, while the no-helmet class accounts for approximately 23.4%.

This imbalance must be considered when splitting the data, training the models, and evaluating performance. The final model should not be selected based only on accuracy. Particular attention should be given to macro F1-score and the model's ability to correctly identify workers who are not wearing helmets.

Concise Observation for the Presentation¶

The dataset contains 4,125 images: 3,161 with helmets (76.6%) and 964 without helmets (23.4%). This class imbalance could cause a model to favor the majority helmet class. Model selection should therefore consider macro precision, macro recall, macro F1-score, confusion matrices, and no-helmet recall rather than accuracy alone.

Data Preprocessing Results and Interpretation¶

Dataset Split Results¶

The original dataset of 4,125 images was divided into training, validation, and test datasets.

The resulting shapes are:

Training:   (3300, 200, 200, 3)  (3300, 1)
Validation: (412, 200, 200, 3)   (412, 1)
Test:       (413, 200, 200, 3)   (413, 1)

The image-array shapes follow this structure:

(number of images, image height, image width, color channels)

Therefore:

  • The training dataset contains 3,300 images.
  • The validation dataset contains 412 images.
  • The test dataset contains 413 images.
  • Every image is 200 pixels high and 200 pixels wide.
  • Every image has three color channels representing red, green, and blue.

The label-array shapes show that each image has one corresponding binary label:

  • Label 0: Without Helmet
  • Label 1: With Helmet

The number of labels matches the number of images in each subset, confirming that the images and labels remained correctly aligned during the split.

Approximate Split Percentages¶

The dataset was divided into approximately:

  • 80% training data
  • 10% validation data
  • 10% test data

The validation and test datasets differ by one image because 825 temporary images cannot be divided evenly into two groups of whole images.

Purpose of the Three Datasets¶

  • The training dataset is used to teach the model and update its weights.
  • The validation dataset is used to evaluate models during development, detect overfitting, and select the best model.
  • The test dataset is reserved for the final evaluation of the selected model on unseen data.

The test data should not be used to choose between models because this could cause information leakage and lead to an overly optimistic performance estimate.

Stratification¶

The split was performed with stratification:

stratify=labels

and:

stratify=y_temp

Stratification preserves approximately the same helmet and no-helmet class proportions in the training, validation, and test datasets. This is important because the dataset contains more helmet images than no-helmet images.

The use of:

random_state=42

makes the split reproducible. Running the code again with the same data and random state should produce the same assignments.

Normalization Results¶

The normalization check produced:

Training range: 0.0 to 1.0
Validation range: 0.0 to 1.0
Test range: 0.0 to 1.0

Before normalization, the image pixels were integers ranging from 0 to 255. Each image array was converted to the float32 data type and divided by 255.0:

X_train_normalized = X_train.astype("float32") / 255.0
X_val_normalized = X_val.astype("float32") / 255.0
X_test_normalized = X_test.astype("float32") / 255.0

This transformation maps the original pixel range to the following normalized range:

[ 0 \leq \text{normalized pixel value} \leq 1 ]

Examples of the transformation include:

[ \frac{0}{255}=0.0 ]

[ \frac{128}{255}\approx0.502 ]

[ \frac{255}{255}=1.0 ]

Therefore:

  • 0.0 represents the lowest possible pixel intensity.
  • Values between 0.0 and 1.0 represent intermediate pixel intensities.
  • 1.0 represents the highest possible pixel intensity.

The output does not mean that every pixel is either 0.0 or 1.0. It means that the smallest pixel value found in each dataset is 0.0, the largest is 1.0, and the remaining pixels have values distributed between those limits.

Why Normalization Is Important¶

Normalization places the input values on a smaller, consistent scale. This can:

  • Improve numerical stability.
  • Help the optimizer update model weights more effectively.
  • Support faster and more stable neural-network training.
  • Prevent large pixel values from producing unnecessarily large intermediate calculations.
  • Ensure that training, validation, and test images use the same numerical scale.

Because the normalization uses the fixed constant 255.0 rather than statistics calculated from the validation or test data, it does not introduce data leakage.

Overall Preprocessing Conclusion¶

The preprocessing process was completed successfully. The 4,125 images were divided into 3,300 training images, 412 validation images, and 413 test images. Each image retained its dimensions of 200 × 200 × 3, and each image remained associated with one binary target label.

The normalization results confirm that the pixel values in all three datasets were successfully converted from the original 0–255 range to the intended 0.0–1.0 range. The data is now appropriately structured and scaled for the CNN and transfer-learning models.

Concise Observation for the Presentation¶

The dataset was divided using a stratified 80% training, 10% validation, and 10% test split, resulting in 3,300, 412, and 413 images, respectively. Each image has dimensions of 200 × 200 × 3. Normalization successfully converted the pixel values from 0–255 to 0.0–1.0 across all three datasets, preparing the images for stable neural-network training and evaluation.

Model Building¶

Utility Functions¶

In [18]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using statsmodels
def model_performance_classification(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # checking which probabilities are greater than threshold
    pred = model.predict(predictors).reshape(-1)>0.5

    target = target.to_numpy().reshape(-1)


    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred, average='macro')  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred, average='macro')  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred, average='macro')  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame({"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1 Score": f1,},index=[0],)

    return df_perf
In [19]:
def plot_confusion_matrix(model,predictors,target,ml=False):
    """
    Function to plot the confusion matrix

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    ml: To specify if the model used is an sklearn ML model or not (True means ML model)
    """

    # checking which probabilities are greater than threshold
    pred = model.predict(predictors).reshape(-1)>0.5

    target = target.to_numpy().reshape(-1)

    # Plotting the Confusion Matrix using confusion matrix() function which is also predefined tensorflow module
    confusion_matrix = tf.math.confusion_matrix(target,pred)
    f, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 8))
    sns.heatmap(
        confusion_matrix,
        annot=True,
        linewidths=.4,
        fmt="d",
        square=True,
        ax=ax
    )
    plt.show()

Model 1: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) from Scratch¶

Let's build a CNN Model.

The model has 2 main parts:

  1. The Feature Extraction layers which are comprised of convolutional and pooling layers.
  2. The Fully Connected classification layers for prediction.

In [20]:
# Initializing Model
model_1 = Sequential()

# Convolutional layers
model_1.add(Conv2D(16, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding="same", input_shape=(200,200,3))) #Complete the code to define the shape of the input image
model_1.add(MaxPooling2D((4, 4), padding='same'))
model_1.add(Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding="same")) #Complete the code to define the number of output channels,the kernel shape and the activation function
model_1.add(MaxPooling2D((2,2), padding='same')) #Complete the code to define the shape of the pooling kernel
model_1.add(Conv2D(64, (3,3), activation='relu', padding="same")) #Complete the code to define the number of output channels,the kernel shape and the activation function

# Flatten and Dense layers
model_1.add(Flatten())
model_1.add(Dense(4, activation='relu'))
model_1.add(Dense(1, activation='relu'))  #Complete the code to define the number of neurons in the output layer and the activation function

Model 1: Convolutional Neural Network from Scratch¶

Important validity note: The current Model 1 results were generated with a ReLU activation in the final output layer. For binary classification with binary cross-entropy, the final layer should use a sigmoid activation. ReLU does not guarantee an output between 0 and 1, so the current results should be treated as provisional. Model 1 should be rebuilt and retrained with Dense(1, activation="sigmoid") before its results are used in the final model comparison.

Model Architecture¶

Model 1 is a convolutional neural network built from scratch for binary helmet classification.

The model contains two principal components:

  1. Feature-extraction layers, consisting of convolutional and pooling operations
  2. Classification layers, consisting of flattened and fully connected dense layers

The model accepts images with the following input shape:

200 × 200 × 3

This represents images that are 200 pixels high, 200 pixels wide, and contain three RGB color channels.

Convolutional and Pooling Layers¶

The first convolutional layer produces 16 feature maps:

(None, 200, 200, 16)

It uses 16 filters with a kernel size of 3 × 3. The spatial dimensions remain 200 × 200 because padding="same" was used.

The first pooling layer reduces the spatial dimensions from:

200 × 200

to:

50 × 50

This reduces computational complexity while retaining prominent visual features.

The second convolutional layer increases the number of feature maps from 16 to 32:

(None, 50, 50, 32)

The second pooling layer reduces the spatial dimensions from:

50 × 50

to:

25 × 25

The third convolutional layer produces 64 feature maps:

(None, 25, 25, 64)

Increasing the number of filters allows the deeper layers to learn more complex visual patterns, such as edges, shapes, colors, head boundaries, and possible helmet features.

Flattening and Classification¶

The final convolutional output contains:

$$ 25 \times 25 \times 64 = 40{,}000 $$

features.

The Flatten layer converts the feature maps into a one-dimensional vector containing 40,000 values.

The first dense layer reduces these features to four neurons:

(None, 4)

The final dense layer contains one neuron:

(None, 1)

The correct output layer for this binary classification problem is:

Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")

A sigmoid activation produces a probability between 0 and 1:

  • Values greater than 0.5 are classified as label 1, With Helmet
  • Values at or below 0.5 are classified as label 0, Without Helmet

Number of Parameters¶

The model contains:

Total parameters:         183,593
Trainable parameters:     183,593
Non-trainable parameters:       0

All 183,593 parameters are trainable because this CNN was built from scratch rather than using pretrained weights.

The convolutional layers contain 23,584 parameters, while the first dense layer contains 160,004 parameters. Therefore, most of the model's parameters are concentrated in the dense classification layer.

Training Configuration¶

The model was trained with:

  • Optimizer: Adam
  • Learning rate: 0.001
  • Loss: Binary cross-entropy
  • Batch size: 32
  • Training epochs: 10
  • Training-data shuffling: Enabled
  • Tracked Keras metric: Recall

With 3,300 training images and a batch size of 32, each epoch contained approximately 104 training steps.

The numerical results below were produced by the original ReLU-output model and must be updated after retraining with a sigmoid output.

Training History¶

Loss¶

Training loss decreased from:

0.7070 in Epoch 1

to:

0.3071 in Epoch 10

This downward trend suggests that the model learned visual patterns from the training data.

Validation loss began at:

0.4046 in Epoch 1

and reached its lowest value of:

0.2131 in Epoch 6

The final validation loss was:

0.2928

The increase after Epoch 6 suggests that additional epochs did not consistently improve validation loss. This could represent normal training variability or the beginning of mild overfitting.

Recall¶

Training recall increased overall from:

88.0% in Epoch 1

to:

94.8% in Epoch 10

Validation recall increased from:

93.4% in Epoch 1

to:

95.9% in Epoch 10

Both training and validation recall remained high but fluctuated across epochs.

Validation recall was frequently higher than training recall. This does not automatically indicate a problem. It can occur when the validation images are easier to classify or because training recall is accumulated while the model's weights are changing throughout an epoch.

Training Performance¶

The provisional post-training metrics were:

Metric Training Result
Accuracy 0.9309
Macro recall 0.8810
Macro precision 0.9211
Macro F1-score 0.8988

The model correctly classified approximately 93.1% of the training images.

The provisional macro F1-score of approximately 89.9% indicates a reasonably strong balance between precision and recall across both classes.

Training Confusion Matrix¶

Actual class Predicted Without Helmet Predicted With Helmet
Without Helmet 607 164
With Helmet 64 2,465

This means:

  • 607 no-helmet images were classified correctly.
  • 164 no-helmet images were incorrectly classified as helmeted.
  • 64 helmet images were incorrectly classified as no-helmet.
  • 2,465 helmet images were classified correctly.
  • The model made 228 training errors.
  • The model made 3,072 correct training predictions.

Training Class-Specific Recall¶

Recall for the Without Helmet class was:

607 ÷ 771 = 78.7%

Recall for the With Helmet class was:

2,465 ÷ 2,529 = 97.5%

The model was considerably better at recognizing helmet images than no-helmet images.

Validation Performance¶

The provisional validation metrics were:

Metric Validation Result
Accuracy 0.9199
Macro recall 0.8753
Macro precision 0.8960
Macro F1-score 0.8850

The model correctly classified approximately 92.0% of the validation images.

The provisional validation macro F1-score was approximately 88.5%, suggesting reasonably balanced overall performance on unseen validation images.

Validation Confusion Matrix¶

Actual class Predicted Without Helmet Predicted With Helmet
Without Helmet 76 20
With Helmet 13 303

This means:

  • 76 no-helmet images were classified correctly.
  • 20 no-helmet images were incorrectly classified as helmeted.
  • 13 helmet images were incorrectly classified as no-helmet.
  • 303 helmet images were classified correctly.
  • The model made 33 validation errors.
  • The model made 379 correct validation predictions.

The validation accuracy can be verified as:

(76 + 303) ÷ 412 = 91.99%

Validation Class-Specific Recall¶

Recall for the Without Helmet class was:

76 ÷ 96 = 79.2%

Recall for the With Helmet class was:

303 ÷ 316 = 95.9%

The model was substantially more effective at recognizing helmet images than no-helmet images.

Safety Interpretation¶

The most consequential validation errors were the 20 workers without helmets who were incorrectly classified as wearing helmets.

These errors represented:

$$ \frac{20}{96}\times100 \approx20.8\% $$

of the actual no-helmet validation images.

In a workplace-safety application, these false helmet detections are especially important because an unsafe worker could be incorrectly identified as compliant.

Although the model achieved approximately 92% validation accuracy, that overall result partially hides its weaker performance on the no-helmet class.

The class imbalance likely contributed to this result because the training data contains more than three times as many helmet images as no-helmet images.

Training-to-Validation Generalization¶

Metric Training Validation Difference
Accuracy 0.9309 0.9199 0.0110
Macro recall 0.8810 0.8753 0.0057
Macro precision 0.9211 0.8960 0.0251
Macro F1-score 0.8988 0.8850 0.0139

The training-validation differences were relatively small.

These gaps suggest that the provisional Model 1 generalized reasonably well and did not demonstrate severe overfitting during the 10 training epochs.

However, validation loss reached its lowest value in Epoch 6 and later increased. Early stopping could potentially preserve the weights associated with the lowest validation loss.

The generalization conclusion must be reevaluated after Model 1 is retrained with the correct sigmoid output activation.

Keras Recall Compared with Macro Recall¶

The final Keras validation recall was:

0.9589

The validation performance table reported macro recall of:

0.8753

These values measure different concepts.

Keras recall treats label 1, With Helmet, as the positive class:

Helmet recall = 303 ÷ 316 = 95.9%

Recall for the no-helmet class was:

No-helmet recall = 76 ÷ 96 = 79.2%

Macro recall gives both classes equal importance:

$$ \text{Macro Recall} = \frac{95.9\%+79.2\%}{2} \approx87.5\% $$

This explains why macro recall is lower than the Keras recall. Macro recall exposes the model's weaker performance on the minority no-helmet class.

Example Predictions¶

The example validation images are blurred and contain limited visual detail. These images demonstrate the difficulty of classifying workers under poor image-quality conditions.

The second prediction must use validation image index 33, matching the displayed image:

prediction = model_1.predict(
    X_val_normalized[33].reshape(1, 200, 200, 3)
)

Using index 12 for both predictions would incorrectly compare the prediction for one image with the true label of another image.

The correctness of the examples should be determined by comparing the printed predicted and true labels after rerunning the corrected model.

Model 1 Conclusion¶

The provisional Model 1 results were:

  • Training accuracy: 93.1%
  • Training macro F1-score: 89.9%
  • Validation accuracy: 92.0%
  • Validation macro F1-score: 88.5%
  • Validation no-helmet recall: 79.2%
  • Validation helmet recall: 95.9%

The small training-validation gap suggests reasonable generalization. However, the model remained considerably better at recognizing helmet images than no-helmet images.

It incorrectly classified 20 of the 96 no-helmet validation images as helmet-compliant, representing approximately 20.8% of the unsafe validation cases.

These results must not be treated as final because the model used an incorrect ReLU output activation. Model 1 should be rebuilt and retrained with a sigmoid output before it is included in the final model comparison.

Required Correction¶

Replace:

model_1.add(Dense(1, activation="relu"))

with:

model_1.add(Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"))

Then rerun:

  1. Model initialization
  2. Optimizer creation
  3. Model compilation
  4. Model summary
  5. Training
  6. Training curve
  7. Training evaluation
  8. Validation evaluation
  9. Confusion matrices
  10. Example predictions
  11. Model comparison tables

Concise Observation for the Presentation¶

Model 1's current results are provisional because the original model used a ReLU output instead of the sigmoid activation required for binary classification. The provisional run achieved 92.0% validation accuracy and an 88.5% macro F1-score, but it correctly detected only 79.2% of no-helmet images. Model 1 must be retrained with a sigmoid output before its results can be compared fairly with the VGG16 models.

Model 2: Transfer Learning with VGG-16 (Base)¶

  • We will be loading a pre-built architecture - VGG16, which was trained on the ImageNet dataset and is the runner-up in the ImageNet competition in 2014.

  • For training VGG16, we will directly use the convolutional and pooling layers and freeze their weights i.e. no training will be done on them. For classification, we will add a Flatten and a single dense layer.

Model 2: VGG16 Base Transfer-Learning Results¶

Model Architecture¶

Model 2 uses the convolutional portion of the pretrained VGG16 network as a feature extractor. VGG16 was originally trained on the ImageNet dataset and learned general visual features such as edges, shapes, textures, and object components.

The model was configured with:

weights="imagenet"
include_top=False
input_shape=(200, 200, 3)

Setting:

include_top=False

removed VGG16's original ImageNet classification layers, allowing the pretrained convolutional base to be adapted to the helmet-classification problem.

All VGG16 layers were frozen:

for layer in vgg_model.layers:
    layer.trainable = False

Therefore, the pretrained VGG16 weights were not changed during training. Only the new binary classification layer was trained.

The VGG16 feature maps were converted into a one-dimensional feature vector using:

Flatten()

A single sigmoid output neuron was added:

Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")

The sigmoid output represents the estimated probability that an image belongs to label 1, With Helmet.

Training Configuration¶

Model 2 was trained using:

  • Optimizer: Adam
  • Learning rate: 0.001
  • Loss: Binary cross-entropy
  • Tracked Keras metric: Recall
  • Batch size: 16
  • Training epochs: 10
  • Feature extractor: Frozen VGG16
  • Data augmentation: None

The training generator used:

shuffle=False

This means that the training images were processed in their existing order. Shuffling would generally be preferable because it changes batch composition across epochs and reduces dependence on the original dataset ordering.

Training History¶

Loss¶

Training loss began at:

0.3410 in Epoch 1

and ended at:

0.1475 in Epoch 10

The lowest reported training loss was:

0.1000 in Epoch 4

Validation loss began at:

0.2274 in Epoch 1

and decreased to:

0.1854 in Epoch 10

The overall decline in validation loss indicates that the model learned useful visual features that generalized to the validation data.

However, training loss fluctuated considerably rather than declining smoothly. The learning rate of 0.001 may have contributed to these fluctuations. A smaller learning rate, such as 0.0001, could produce more gradual updates in a future transfer-learning experiment.

Recall¶

Training recall varied between approximately:

90.9% and 100.0%

Validation recall varied between approximately:

90.8% and 97.8%

The final validation recall was:

96.2%

This means that the final model correctly identified approximately 96.2% of the validation images belonging to label 1, With Helmet.

The recall curves fluctuated noticeably across epochs. Although both training and validation recall remained high, the lack of a smooth trend demonstrates why recall alone should not be used to select the final model.

Training Performance¶

The post-training evaluation produced:

Metric Training Result
Accuracy 0.9745
Macro recall 0.9586
Macro precision 0.9698
Macro F1-score 0.9640

The model correctly classified approximately 97.5% of the training images.

The macro F1-score of approximately 96.4% indicates strong performance across both classes on the training dataset.

Training Confusion Matrix¶

Actual class Predicted Without Helmet Predicted With Helmet
Without Helmet 716 55
With Helmet 29 2,500

This means:

  • 716 no-helmet images were correctly classified.
  • 55 no-helmet images were incorrectly classified as helmeted.
  • 29 helmet images were incorrectly classified as no-helmet.
  • 2,500 helmet images were correctly classified.
  • The model made 84 training errors.
  • The model made 3,216 correct training predictions.

Training Class-Specific Recall¶

Recall for the Without Helmet class was:

716 ÷ 771 = 92.9%

Recall for the With Helmet class was:

2,500 ÷ 2,529 = 98.9%

The model performed extremely well on both classes in the training dataset, although helmet recall remained higher than no-helmet recall.

Validation Performance¶

The validation evaluation produced:

Metric Validation Result
Accuracy 0.9199
Macro recall 0.8716
Macro precision 0.8987
Macro F1-score 0.8841

The model correctly classified approximately 92.0% of the validation images.

The validation macro F1-score was approximately 88.4%, which was notably lower than the training macro F1-score of 96.4%.

Validation Confusion Matrix¶

Actual class Predicted Without Helmet Predicted With Helmet
Without Helmet 75 21
With Helmet 12 304

This means:

  • 75 no-helmet images were correctly classified.
  • 21 no-helmet images were incorrectly classified as helmeted.
  • 12 helmet images were incorrectly classified as no-helmet.
  • 304 helmet images were correctly classified.
  • The model made 33 validation errors.
  • The model made 379 correct validation predictions.

The validation accuracy can be verified as:

(75 + 304) ÷ 412 = 91.99%

Validation Class-Specific Recall¶

Recall for the Without Helmet class was:

75 ÷ 96 = 78.1%

Recall for the With Helmet class was:

304 ÷ 316 = 96.2%

The model was therefore substantially better at detecting helmet images than no-helmet images.

Safety Interpretation¶

The most consequential validation error was the group of 21 workers without helmets who were incorrectly classified as wearing helmets.

These errors represented:

$$ \frac{21}{96}\times100 \approx 21.9\% $$

of the actual no-helmet validation images.

In an operational safety-monitoring system, these errors could allow unsafe workers to pass through the system without being flagged.

The 12 helmet images incorrectly classified as no-helmet would generate false alarms. Although these cases could require unnecessary human review, they are generally less safety-critical than failing to flag an unprotected worker.

The overall validation accuracy of approximately 92% partially hides this weakness because the dataset contains considerably more helmet images than no-helmet images.

Evidence of Overfitting¶

The differences between training and validation performance were:

Metric Training Validation Difference
Accuracy 0.9745 0.9199 0.0546
Macro recall 0.9586 0.8716 0.0870
Macro precision 0.9698 0.8987 0.0711
Macro F1-score 0.9640 0.8841 0.0799

The training macro F1-score was approximately eight percentage points higher than the validation macro F1-score.

The largest decline was in macro recall, which decreased by approximately 8.7 percentage points.

These gaps indicate that Model 2 learned the training data substantially better than it generalized to unseen validation images. The results therefore provide evidence of overfitting.

Although the frozen VGG16 features are powerful, the trained classification layer appears to fit the training data more effectively than the validation data.

Keras Recall Compared with Macro Recall¶

The final Keras validation recall was:

0.9620

The validation performance table reported macro recall of:

0.8716

These values measure different concepts.

Keras recall treats label 1, With Helmet, as the positive class:

Helmet recall = 304 ÷ 316 = 96.2%

Recall for the no-helmet class was:

No-helmet recall = 75 ÷ 96 = 78.1%

Macro recall averages the recall values for both classes:

$$ \text{Macro Recall} = \frac{96.2\%+78.1\%}{2} \approx87.2\% $$

This explains why macro recall is substantially lower than the Keras recall.

Macro recall is more informative for this imbalanced dataset because it gives equal importance to the helmet and no-helmet classes.

Interpretation of the Example Images¶

Validation images 12 and 33 are blurred and contain limited visual detail. Image 33 appears to contain a yellow safety helmet, while image 12 is substantially more ambiguous.

These examples demonstrate the difficulty of classifying low-resolution images.

The displayed image, normalized input, and true label must use the same index. The correctness of each prediction should be determined by comparing its printed predicted label with its printed true label.

The images alone do not provide enough information to establish whether both model predictions were correct.

Model 2 Conclusion¶

Model 2 achieved:

  • 97.5% training accuracy
  • 96.4% training macro F1-score
  • 92.0% validation accuracy
  • 88.4% validation macro F1-score

The sizable training-validation gaps indicate overfitting.

The model correctly detected approximately:

  • 96.2% of helmet validation images
  • 78.1% of no-helmet validation images

It incorrectly classified 21 of the 96 unsafe no-helmet validation cases as helmet-compliant.

Therefore, Model 2 should not be selected based only on its overall accuracy or label-1 recall. It should be compared with the remaining models using:

  • Validation macro F1-score
  • Macro recall
  • No-helmet recall
  • Confusion matrices
  • Training-validation performance gaps
  • Number of unsafe false-compliance errors

Concise Observation for the Presentation¶

The frozen VGG16 base achieved 97.5% training accuracy but only 92.0% validation accuracy, indicating overfitting. Validation macro F1-score was 88.4%. The model identified 96.2% of helmet images but only 78.1% of no-helmet images, incorrectly classifying 21 of 96 unsafe cases as helmet-compliant. These results demonstrate why overall accuracy and standard label-1 recall overstate the model's effectiveness for safety monitoring.

Model 3: Transfer Learning with VGG-16 (Base + FFNN)¶

  • We will directly use the convolutional and pooling layers and freeze their weights i.e. no training will be done on them. For classification, we will add a Flatten layer and a Feed Forward Neural Network.

Model 3: VGG16 Base with a Feed-Forward Neural Network¶

Model Configuration¶

Model 3 uses the frozen VGG16 convolutional base as a pretrained feature extractor. The original VGG16 classification layers were removed and replaced with a custom feed-forward neural network.

The classification head contained:

  • A Flatten layer
  • A dense layer with 64 neurons and ReLU activation
  • A dropout layer with a rate of 0.30
  • A dense layer with 32 neurons and ReLU activation
  • One sigmoid output neuron for binary classification

The VGG16 layers remained frozen, so only the custom dense classification layers were trained.

The model used:

  • Optimizer: Adam
  • Learning rate: 0.0001
  • Loss: Binary cross-entropy
  • Batch size: 16
  • Training epochs: 10
  • Tracked Keras metric: Recall
  • Data augmentation: None

The dropout layer randomly deactivated 30% of its inputs during training to reduce dependence on individual features and potentially limit overfitting.

Training note: The generator used shuffle=False, meaning the images were processed in the same order during training. Shuffling would generally be preferable because it changes the batch composition across epochs.

Training History¶

Loss¶

Training loss began at 0.4477 in Epoch 1 and ended at 0.2265 in Epoch 10.

Validation loss decreased from 0.3202 to 0.2128. The lowest validation loss was approximately 0.2074 in Epoch 8.

The decline in validation loss indicates that the model learned features that generalized to unseen validation images. The slight increase after Epoch 8 suggests that further training did not consistently improve validation loss.

Recall¶

Training recall and validation recall remained high but fluctuated across epochs.

Training recall ranged from approximately:

84.6% to 100.0%

Validation recall ranged from approximately:

93.0% to 99.1%

The final validation recall was:

98.1%

This Keras recall measures only label 1, With Helmet. It does not directly measure how effectively the model identifies workers without helmets.

The volatility in the recall curves indicates that recall alone should not be used to select the final model. Macro metrics and confusion matrices provide a more balanced assessment.

Training Performance¶

The final training metrics were:

Metric Training Result
Accuracy 0.9470
Macro recall 0.9054
Macro precision 0.9437
Macro F1-score 0.9227

The model correctly classified approximately 94.7% of the 3,300 training images.

Training Confusion Matrix¶

Actual class Predicted Without Helmet Predicted With Helmet
Without Helmet 638 133
With Helmet 42 2,487

This means:

  • 638 no-helmet images were classified correctly.
  • 133 no-helmet images were incorrectly classified as helmeted.
  • 42 helmet images were incorrectly classified as no-helmet.
  • 2,487 helmet images were classified correctly.
  • The model made 175 training errors.
  • The model made 3,125 correct training predictions.

Training Class-Specific Recall¶

Recall for the Without Helmet class was:

638 ÷ 771 = 82.7%

Recall for the With Helmet class was:

2,487 ÷ 2,529 = 98.3%

The model was considerably better at recognizing helmet images than no-helmet images, even on the training dataset.

Validation Performance¶

The validation metrics were:

Metric Validation Result
Accuracy 0.9199
Macro recall 0.8499
Macro precision 0.9199
Macro F1-score 0.8782

The model correctly classified approximately 92.0% of the 412 validation images.

Validation Confusion Matrix¶

Actual class Predicted Without Helmet Predicted With Helmet
Without Helmet 69 27
With Helmet 6 310

This means:

  • 69 no-helmet images were classified correctly.
  • 27 no-helmet images were incorrectly classified as helmeted.
  • 6 helmet images were incorrectly classified as no-helmet.
  • 310 helmet images were classified correctly.
  • The model made 33 validation errors.
  • The model made 379 correct validation predictions.

The validation accuracy can be verified as:

(69 + 310) ÷ 412 = 92.0%

Validation Class-Specific Recall¶

Recall for the Without Helmet class was:

69 ÷ 96 = 71.9%

Recall for the With Helmet class was:

310 ÷ 316 = 98.1%

The model was much more effective at identifying helmet images than no-helmet images.

Safety Interpretation¶

The most consequential errors were the 27 no-helmet images incorrectly classified as helmeted.

These errors represented:

$$ \frac{27}{96}\times100 \approx 28.1\% $$

of the actual no-helmet validation images.

In practical terms, Model 3 failed to flag more than one out of every four no-helmet images in the validation dataset.

Although Model 3 achieved approximately 92% validation accuracy and very high macro precision, those metrics conceal its weak detection of the minority no-helmet class.

The model produced only six false alarms on helmet images, but it did so by favoring the With Helmet prediction. This reduced false alarms while increasing the number of unsafe no-helmet cases incorrectly classified as compliant.

Training-to-Validation Generalization¶

Metric Training Validation Difference
Accuracy 0.9470 0.9199 0.0271
Macro recall 0.9054 0.8499 0.0556
Macro precision 0.9437 0.9199 0.0238
Macro F1-score 0.9227 0.8782 0.0445

Validation performance was approximately two to six percentage points lower than training performance.

The largest decline occurred in macro recall. This indicates that the model generalized less effectively across both classes, particularly for the minority no-helmet class.

The training-validation gap provides evidence of moderate overfitting, even with the 30% dropout layer.

Keras Recall Compared with Macro Recall¶

The final Keras validation recall was:

0.9810

The validation performance table reported macro recall of:

0.8499

These values measure different concepts.

Keras recall treats label 1, With Helmet, as the positive class:

Helmet recall = 310 ÷ 316 = 98.1%

Recall for the no-helmet class was:

No-helmet recall = 69 ÷ 96 = 71.9%

Macro recall gives both classes equal importance:

$$ \text{Macro Recall} = \frac{98.1\%+71.9\%}{2} \approx85.0\% $$

This explains why the macro recall is substantially lower than the Keras recall.

The result also demonstrates why standard Keras recall can be misleading for this project: it emphasizes the majority helmet class rather than the more safety-critical no-helmet class.

Comparison with Model 2¶

Models 2 and 3 achieved the same validation accuracy:

91.99%

However, their error patterns differed:

Metric Model 2 Model 3
Validation accuracy 0.9199 0.9199
Macro recall 0.8716 0.8499
Macro precision 0.8987 0.9199
Macro F1-score 0.8841 0.8782
No-helmet cases missed 21 27
Helmet false alarms 12 6

Adding the feed-forward neural network increased macro precision and reduced false alarms on helmet images. However, it also increased the number of unsafe no-helmet cases incorrectly classified as helmeted.

Model 3 therefore traded recall for precision. That tradeoff is not desirable for this safety application because failing to identify an unprotected worker is more consequential than generating an additional review alert.

Example Validation Images¶

Validation images 12 and 33 are blurred and contain limited visual detail. These images demonstrate the difficulty of classifying low-resolution and ambiguous examples.

The displayed images, normalized inputs, and true labels use consistent indices. The correctness of each prediction should be determined by comparing its printed predicted label with its printed true label.

The image alone should not be used to conclude whether the model prediction was correct, particularly for the heavily blurred example.

Model 3 Conclusion¶

Model 3 achieved:

  • 94.7% training accuracy
  • 92.0% validation accuracy
  • 92.0% validation macro precision
  • 87.8% validation macro F1-score

The model demonstrated high precision and excellent helmet recall. However, its validation recall for no-helmet images was only 71.9%.

The model incorrectly classified 27 of the 96 no-helmet validation images as helmet-compliant, representing approximately 28.1% of the unsafe validation cases.

The addition of the feed-forward neural network improved precision but produced a less balanced result than Model 2. Model 3 should therefore not be selected solely because it achieved the highest validation precision.

For this safety application, macro F1-score, macro recall, no-helmet recall, and the number of unsafe false-compliance errors provide stronger selection criteria.

Concise Observation for the Presentation¶

Model 3 achieved 92.0% validation accuracy and the highest validation macro precision at 92.0%. However, validation macro recall declined to 85.0%, and the model correctly identified only 71.9% of no-helmet images. It incorrectly classified 27 of 96 unsafe cases as helmet-compliant. The FFNN reduced false alarms but increased missed safety violations, making Model 3 less suitable than a more balanced model.

Model 4: Transfer Learning with VGG-16 (Base + FFNN + Data Augmentation)¶

  • In most of the real-world case studies, it is challenging to acquire a large number of images and then train CNNs.

  • To overcome this problem, one approach we might consider is Data Augmentation.

  • CNNs have the property of translational invariance, which means they can recognise an object even if its appearance shifts translationally in some way. - Taking this attribute into account, we can augment the images using the techniques listed below

    • Horizontal Flip (should be set to True/False)
    • Vertical Flip (should be set to True/False)
    • Height Shift (should be between 0 and 1)
    • Width Shift (should be between 0 and 1)
    • Rotation (should be between 0 and 180)
    • Shear (should be between 0 and 1)
    • Zoom (should be between 0 and 1) etc.

Remember, data augmentation should not be used in the validation/test data set.

    round(helmet_probability, 4)
)
print("Predicted Label:", predicted_label)
print("True Label:", true_label)
print(
    "Prediction Correct:",
    predicted_label == true_label
)

Model 4: VGG16 with FFNN and Data Augmentation¶

Model Configuration¶

Model 4 combines:

  • A pretrained VGG16 convolutional base
  • A feed-forward neural network classification head
  • Data augmentation applied only to the training images

The VGG16 layers were frozen, so their pretrained ImageNet weights were not changed during training.

The classification head contained:

  • A Flatten layer
  • A dense layer with 64 neurons and ReLU activation
  • A dropout layer with a rate of 0.30
  • A dense layer with 32 neurons and ReLU activation
  • One sigmoid output neuron for binary classification

The model used:

  • Optimizer: Adam
  • Learning rate: 0.0001
  • Loss: Binary cross-entropy
  • Batch size: 16
  • Tracked Keras metric: Recall

Data Augmentation¶

The training images were augmented using:

  • Rotation of up to 15 degrees
  • Horizontal shifting of up to 10%
  • Vertical shifting of up to 10%
  • Shearing of up to 10%
  • Zooming of up to 10%
  • Horizontal flipping
  • No vertical flipping

These transformations exposed the model to additional variation in worker position, image framing, camera angle, and orientation.

Only the training images were augmented. The validation and test images remained unchanged so that they could provide realistic evaluations of model performance.

Important training note: Model 4 was trained in two consecutive calls to model.fit(), with 10 epochs in each call. Because the model was not rebuilt between the calls, the current results represent 20 total training epochs. The results should therefore be considered provisional when comparing Model 4 with models trained for only 10 epochs.

Training Performance¶

The final training metrics were:

Metric Training Result
Accuracy 0.9521
Macro recall 0.9322
Macro precision 0.9338
Macro F1-score 0.9330

The model correctly classified approximately 95.2% of the 3,300 training images.

Training Confusion Matrix¶

Actual class Predicted Without Helmet Predicted With Helmet
Without Helmet 690 81
With Helmet 77 2,452

This means:

  • 690 no-helmet images were classified correctly.
  • 81 no-helmet images were incorrectly classified as helmeted.
  • 77 helmet images were incorrectly classified as no-helmet.
  • 2,452 helmet images were classified correctly.
  • The model made 158 training errors.
  • The model made 3,142 correct training predictions.

Class-specific training recall was:

  • Without Helmet: 690 ÷ 771 = 89.5%
  • With Helmet: 2,452 ÷ 2,529 = 97.0%

The model performed better on helmet images than no-helmet images, even on the training dataset.

Validation Performance¶

The validation metrics were:

Metric Validation Result
Accuracy 0.9248
Macro recall 0.8893
Macro precision 0.8981
Macro F1-score 0.8936

The model correctly classified approximately 92.5% of the 412 validation images.

Validation Confusion Matrix¶

Actual class Predicted Without Helmet Predicted With Helmet
Without Helmet 79 17
With Helmet 14 302

This means:

  • 79 no-helmet images were classified correctly.
  • 17 no-helmet images were incorrectly classified as helmeted.
  • 14 helmet images were incorrectly classified as no-helmet.
  • 302 helmet images were classified correctly.
  • The model made 31 validation errors.
  • The model made 381 correct validation predictions.

Class-specific validation recall was:

  • Without Helmet: 79 ÷ 96 = 82.3%
  • With Helmet: 302 ÷ 316 = 95.6%

The model was substantially better at recognizing helmet images than no-helmet images.

Safety Interpretation¶

The most consequential validation errors were the 17 no-helmet images incorrectly classified as helmeted.

These errors represented:

$$ \frac{17}{96}\times100 \approx 17.7\% $$

of the actual no-helmet validation images.

In an operational safety-monitoring system, these cases could represent workers who are not wearing helmets but are incorrectly identified as compliant.

Training-to-Validation Generalization¶

Metric Training Validation Difference
Accuracy 0.9521 0.9248 0.0274
Macro recall 0.9322 0.8893 0.0429
Macro precision 0.9338 0.8981 0.0357
Macro F1-score 0.9330 0.8936 0.0394

Validation performance was approximately three to four percentage points lower than training performance. This indicates some overfitting, although Model 4 generalized better than the VGG16 base model without augmentation.

The comparison must be interpreted cautiously because Model 4 was accidentally trained for 20 total epochs.

Model Comparison¶

The validation results for all four models were:

Model Accuracy Macro Recall Macro Precision Macro F1
CNN from Scratch 0.9199 0.8753 0.8960 0.8850
VGG16 Base 0.9199 0.8716 0.8987 0.8841
VGG16 Base + FFNN 0.9199 0.8499 0.9199 0.8782
VGG16 Base + FFNN + Augmentation 0.9248 0.8893 0.8981 0.8936

Model 4 achieved the highest:

  • Validation accuracy
  • Validation macro recall
  • Validation macro F1-score

Model 3 achieved the highest macro precision, but its lower recall and F1-score indicated less balanced performance.

Based on the available validation evidence, Model 4 was selected for final test evaluation.

Test Performance¶

The provisional Model 4 test metrics were:

Metric Test Result
Accuracy 0.8910
Macro recall 0.8538
Macro precision 0.8465
Macro F1-score 0.8500

The model correctly classified approximately 89.1% of the 413 test images.

Test Confusion Matrix¶

Actual class Predicted Without Helmet Predicted With Helmet
Without Helmet 76 21
With Helmet 24 292

This means:

  • 76 no-helmet images were classified correctly.
  • 21 no-helmet images were incorrectly classified as helmeted.
  • 24 helmet images were incorrectly classified as no-helmet.
  • 292 helmet images were classified correctly.
  • The model made 45 test errors.
  • The model made 368 correct test predictions.

Class-specific test recall was:

  • Without Helmet: 76 ÷ 97 = 78.4%
  • With Helmet: 292 ÷ 316 = 92.4%

The model remained more effective at detecting helmet images than no-helmet images.

Test Safety Interpretation¶

The model incorrectly classified 21 of the 97 no-helmet test images as helmeted.

This represents:

$$ \frac{21}{97}\times100 \approx 21.6\% $$

of the unsafe no-helmet test cases.

At the default probability threshold of 0.5, the model failed to flag approximately one out of every five no-helmet images in this test sample.

The 24 helmet images classified as no-helmet would create false alarms. These errors could increase the need for human review, but they are generally less safety-critical than failing to identify an unprotected worker.

Validation-to-Test Generalization¶

Metric Validation Test Decline
Accuracy 0.9248 0.8910 0.0337
Macro recall 0.8893 0.8538 0.0355
Macro precision 0.8981 0.8465 0.0516
Macro F1-score 0.8936 0.8500 0.0436

Test performance was approximately three to five percentage points lower than validation performance.

This indicates that the validation results somewhat overestimated performance on the independent test set. Nevertheless, the test accuracy remained above the 76.6% majority-class baseline.

Keras Recall Compared with Macro Recall¶

Keras recall treats label 1, With Helmet, as the positive class. It primarily measures how effectively the model recognizes helmet images.

Macro recall calculates recall separately for both classes and gives them equal weight.

For the test dataset:

  • No-helmet recall: 78.4%
  • Helmet recall: 92.4%

Therefore:

$$ \text{Macro Recall} = \frac{78.4\%+92.4\%}{2} \approx85.4\% $$

This explains why macro recall is lower than the Keras recall reported for the helmet class.

Macro recall provides a more balanced assessment because it gives equal importance to the helmet and no-helmet classes.

Overall Model 4 Conclusion¶

Model 4 produced the strongest provisional validation results among the four models:

  • Validation accuracy: 92.5%
  • Validation macro recall: 88.9%
  • Validation macro F1-score: 89.4%

Its provisional test results were:

  • Test accuracy: 89.1%
  • Test macro recall: 85.4%
  • Test macro precision: 84.6%
  • Test macro F1-score: 85.0%

Data augmentation appears to have improved validation performance relative to the non-augmented VGG16 models. However, Model 4 remained significantly better at identifying helmet images than unsafe no-helmet images.

The principal operational limitation is that the model incorrectly classified approximately 21.6% of no-helmet test images as helmet-compliant. The model should therefore not be used as the sole safety-enforcement mechanism without additional evaluation and human oversight.

Recommended Next Steps¶

  1. Rebuild Model 4 and train it once for 10 epochs to ensure a controlled comparison.
  2. Do not change the model configuration based on the previously viewed test results.
  3. Evaluate alternative probability thresholds using validation data.
  4. Collect additional no-helmet images to reduce class imbalance.
  5. Add more blurred, obstructed, distant, and low-light training examples.
  6. Route low-confidence predictions to a human reviewer.
  7. Test performance across different sites, cameras, lighting conditions, worker populations, and helmet styles.
  8. Monitor no-helmet recall and false-compliance errors after deployment.
  9. Use the model as a decision-support tool rather than an autonomous enforcement system.

Concise Observation for the Presentation¶

Model 4 achieved the strongest provisional validation performance, with 92.5% accuracy and an 89.4% macro F1-score. Test performance declined to 89.1% accuracy and an 85.0% macro F1-score. The model correctly identified 92.4% of helmet images but only 78.4% of no-helmet images, incorrectly classifying 21 of 97 unsafe test cases as helmet-compliant. Additional minority-class data, threshold optimization, and human review are recommended before operational use.

Actionable Insights & Recommendations¶

Actionable Insights and Recommendations¶

Provisional Final Model Selection¶

Model 4, VGG16 Base with FFNN and Data Augmentation, produced the strongest available validation results.

Its validation performance was:

Metric Validation Result
Accuracy 0.9248
Macro recall 0.8893
Macro precision 0.8981
Macro F1-score 0.8936

Model 4 achieved the highest validation accuracy, macro recall, and macro F1-score among the four evaluated models. It therefore provided the strongest balance between overall classification performance and class-specific recall.

However, this selection must be considered provisional for two reasons:

  1. Model 1 was originally trained with a ReLU output instead of the sigmoid activation required for binary classification.
  2. Model 4 was trained in two consecutive 10-epoch calls, resulting in 20 total epochs, while the other models were trained for 10 epochs.

A controlled comparison requires Model 1 to be rebuilt with a sigmoid output and Model 4 to be rebuilt and trained once for 10 epochs.

The model architecture and hyperparameters should not be adjusted based on the test results that have already been observed.

Provisional Test Performance¶

The provisional Model 4 test results were:

Metric Test Result
Accuracy 0.8910
Macro recall 0.8538
Macro precision 0.8465
Macro F1-score 0.8500

The model correctly classified:

368 of 413 test images

and made:

45 test errors

Although the test accuracy exceeded the 76.6% majority-class baseline, performance declined relative to validation results.

Metric Validation Test Decline
Accuracy 0.9248 0.8910 0.0337
Macro recall 0.8893 0.8538 0.0355
Macro precision 0.8981 0.8465 0.0516
Macro F1-score 0.8936 0.8500 0.0436

This decline indicates that validation performance somewhat overestimated performance on the independent test dataset.

Safety Implications¶

Overall accuracy should not be considered alone because the dataset contains substantially more helmet images than no-helmet images.

The final test confusion matrix showed:

Actual class Predicted Without Helmet Predicted With Helmet
Without Helmet 76 21
With Helmet 24 292

Therefore:

  • 76 no-helmet images were classified correctly.
  • 21 no-helmet images were incorrectly classified as helmeted.
  • 24 helmet images were incorrectly classified as no-helmet.
  • 292 helmet images were classified correctly.

No-Helmet Detection¶

No-helmet recall was:

76 ÷ 97 = 78.4%

The model incorrectly classified:

21 ÷ 97 = 21.6%

of the actual no-helmet test images as helmet-compliant.

This is the most consequential error because it may allow an unsafe condition to go undetected.

Helmet Detection¶

Helmet recall was:

292 ÷ 316 = 92.4%

The model was therefore substantially more effective at recognizing helmet images than no-helmet images.

The 24 helmet images classified as no-helmet would generate false alarms and unnecessary reviews. However, these errors are generally less safety-critical than incorrectly declaring an unprotected worker compliant.

Primary Operational Finding¶

At the default probability threshold of 0.5, the model failed to flag approximately one out of every five no-helmet test images.

This error rate is too high for the model to serve as the sole safety-enforcement mechanism.

Key Actionable Insights¶

1. Overall accuracy overstates operational effectiveness¶

The model achieved 89.1% test accuracy, but no-helmet recall was only 78.4%. The class imbalance allows strong overall accuracy even when the model misses a meaningful percentage of unsafe cases.

Model evaluation should prioritize:

  • No-helmet recall
  • Macro recall
  • Macro F1-score
  • Number of unsafe false-compliance errors
  • Training-validation-test consistency

2. Standard Keras recall measures the less critical class¶

Because label 1 represents With Helmet, the standard Keras recall metric measures helmet recall.

It does not directly measure the model's ability to detect workers without helmets.

The project should continue reporting:

  • Helmet recall
  • No-helmet recall
  • Macro recall
  • Confusion matrices

3. Data augmentation improved validation performance but did not eliminate the safety gap¶

Model 4 achieved the strongest validation macro F1-score, suggesting that augmentation helped the model generalize across variations in image position, framing, and orientation.

However, data augmentation did not eliminate the model's weaker performance on no-helmet images.

4. Image quality is a material source of risk¶

The dataset includes blurred, obstructed, distant, poorly framed, and low-resolution images. These conditions can make helmet status difficult to determine even for a human reviewer.

Image-quality checks should be incorporated into any future system so that unreadable images are not treated as confident compliance decisions.

5. Whole-image classification may not be sufficient for real deployment¶

The current models classify an entire image as With Helmet or Without Helmet. They do not locate individual workers or determine helmet status separately for each person.

This creates a limitation when:

  • An image contains multiple workers.
  • Some workers are wearing helmets and others are not.
  • A helmet appears in the background.
  • The relevant worker occupies only a small part of the image.

A production system may require person detection followed by person-level helmet classification or an object-detection model that localizes both workers and helmets.

Recommendations¶

1. Correct and rerun the model comparison¶

Before finalizing the academic comparison:

  • Rebuild Model 1 with Dense(1, activation="sigmoid").
  • Rebuild Model 4 from its initial weights.
  • Train Model 4 once for 10 epochs.
  • Regenerate all training and validation metrics.
  • Recreate the model-comparison tables.
  • Confirm the final model using validation results only.

2. Prioritize no-helmet recall in model selection¶

The final selection criterion should explicitly consider unsafe false-compliance errors.

If two models have similar macro F1-scores, preference should be given to the model that:

  • Correctly identifies more no-helmet images.
  • Misclassifies fewer unprotected workers as compliant.
  • Maintains an acceptable false-alarm rate.
  • Demonstrates a smaller generalization gap.

3. Evaluate a more conservative probability threshold¶

The current decision threshold is:

0.5

Because label 1 means With Helmet, the model declares compliance whenever the helmet probability exceeds 0.5.

A higher helmet threshold would require stronger evidence before declaring a worker compliant. This could improve no-helmet recall and reduce unsafe false-compliance errors, although it would also generate more false alarms.

Alternative thresholds must be selected using validation data—not test data.

4. Address the class imbalance¶

The training dataset contains substantially fewer no-helmet images than helmet images.

Future training should consider:

  • Collecting additional no-helmet images
  • Class-weighted binary cross-entropy
  • Balanced batch sampling
  • Carefully controlled minority-class augmentation
  • Reporting class-specific performance after each experiment

5. Improve data quality and label quality¶

Future data collection should include more representative examples involving:

  • Low-light environments
  • Blurred images
  • Partial occlusion
  • Distant workers
  • Side and rear views
  • Different helmet colors and styles
  • Different work sites and camera systems
  • Multiple workers in one image

Ambiguous or severely blurred images should be reviewed for labeling accuracy.

6. Use human review for uncertain cases¶

The model should operate as a decision-support system rather than an autonomous enforcement mechanism.

Images should be routed to a human reviewer when:

  • Helmet probability is close to the decision threshold.
  • Image quality is poor.
  • Multiple workers are present.
  • The worker's head is obstructed.
  • The model and an image-quality check disagree.

7. Validate across operational environments¶

Before deployment, the model should be evaluated across:

  • Different construction and industrial sites
  • Different camera positions and resolutions
  • Indoor and outdoor lighting conditions
  • Different weather conditions
  • Different worker populations
  • Different helmet colors and designs

Performance on one dataset does not establish reliability across all workplaces.

8. Monitor performance after deployment¶

Ongoing monitoring should include:

  • No-helmet recall
  • Unsafe false-compliance rate
  • False-alarm rate
  • Confidence-score distribution
  • Image-quality failures
  • Performance drift over time
  • Performance differences across sites and operating conditions

Periodic human audits should identify emerging failure patterns and determine when retraining is required.

9. Maintain privacy and governance controls¶

Workplace image monitoring should include:

  • Appropriate access controls
  • Defined image-retention periods
  • Secure data storage
  • Documented authorized uses
  • Worker notification where required
  • Periodic privacy and governance reviews

Final Conclusion¶

The project demonstrates that CNNs and transfer learning can classify helmet use from workplace images. Model 4 produced the strongest provisional validation performance and achieved 89.1% test accuracy with an 85.0% macro F1-score.

However, the model correctly identified only 78.4% of no-helmet test images and incorrectly classified 21 of 97 unsafe cases as helmet-compliant.

These results demonstrate that strong overall accuracy does not guarantee reliable safety performance. The current model shows potential as a screening and decision-support tool, but it is not ready to serve as an autonomous safety-enforcement system.

The final deployment decision should prioritize:

  • No-helmet recall
  • Unsafe false-compliance errors
  • Balanced class performance
  • External validation
  • Human review
  • Continuous monitoring
  • Privacy and governance controls

Concise Recommendation for the Presentation¶

Model 4 produced the strongest provisional validation performance, but it missed 21.6% of no-helmet test cases. SafeGuard Corp should use the model only as a human-supervised screening tool while improving minority-class representation, evaluating a more conservative compliance threshold, expanding person-level detection capabilities, and validating performance across operational environments.

Power Ahead!
